column2: The “parent” report is only the parent company itself; from subsidiaries, only the profit they paid out to the parent is counted. Dividends are paid on the basis of this report.
The “consolidated” report shows the whole group as one company; the subsidiaries’ debts and losses aren’t hidden.
If consolidated profit is always much lower than parent profit, the group is weaker than it looks.
A common mistake: adding parent profit to the subsidiaries’ profit; the same profit gets counted twice.
If the father of a family earns well but the children borrow every month, the whole family is worse off than the father.
A holding’s net asset value (NAV) = the value of its shares and assets − debts − tax on selling, divided by the number of shares.
Take the numbers from the monthly portfolio report on Codal.
Many holdings trade below NAV; this discount is only an opportunity when managers pass that value on to shareholders through dividends or asset sales.
A wallet with 1 million inside sold for 800 thousand is only a good deal if you can open it.
Many companies’ profit depends on decisions outside the company:
The dollar rate an exporter really gets, sales discounts because of sanctions, dollar debts owed to it that haven’t come back, and dollar debt when the dollar jumps.
A government-set product price, feedstock and energy prices, government mining royalties, export duties or bans.
Summer power cuts and winter gas cuts, and the return on government bonds.
A taxi driver’s fares are set by petrol prices, the city-approved fare and the traffic scheme; none of them is in the driver’s hands.
Factors outside the company
For each share write one sentence: “If the government made one bad decision tomorrow, what would it be and what percentage of profit would it take?”
A company whose profit depends on one government decision should be bought cheaper so you have room for error.
If your shop’s income depends on a temporary city licence, you buy it cheaper than a shop with a permanent licence.
Options aren’t a main FIS tool.
A sensible use: a put option as temporary insurance on a share you own.
Buying and selling options to speculate, without understanding margin and leverage, is the same risk of ruin.
An embedded put option sets a floor on the loss, but check who guarantees it.
You buy car insurance for safety, not to make money from accidents.
The debt-to-equity ratio is misleading in Iran, because shareholders’ equity is recorded with old numbers.
Better: divide bank debt by operating profit; that is, how many years of profit pay off the debt.

Article 141: if accumulated losses exceed half the capital, the meeting must decide whether to wind up or continue. It is usually “solved” with a capital increase from revaluation, without the real problem being fixed.
To know whether your loan payments are too high, you compare them with your yearly income, not with the old price of your house.
Debt and Article 141
A bank’s profit = the gap between the interest it takes from borrowers and pays to depositors + fees − loans that don’t come back.
A bank’s properties and loans that are only rolled over can hide real losses. Banks are the riskiest group for beginners.
Insurers: compare the claims paid with the premiums taken, and look at the investment profit on their reserves.
A family loan fund is healthy when loans come back; if they only give new loans so the old ones get paid off, the problem is hidden.
Tax: the normal rate is 25%, with exemptions such as exports. Take the real rate and when the exemption ends from the tax note.
The main owner: if it needs money, it wants high dividends; if it owes the company money, that’s a warning bell.
Expert revaluation reports on Codal are a free source for the value of land and machines.
If after 6 to 12 months your pretend portfolio does worse than a simple fund, that’s useful information, not failure.
If after a year of practising cooking, the restaurant on the corner is still better and cheaper, knowing that is valuable.
